metadata.title: Member realism ratings for simulated counselling conversations
metadata.description: Human judgements of whether simulated members (patients) in text-based counselling conversations read as written by a real person. Conversations were generated by three member simulators against three counsellor models. The annotation study also contained human-written conversations and further counsellor configurations; those are not part of this release.

systems.ours: the simulator proposed in this work

metadata.protocol: Three annotators rated member turns in a blind interface. They were not told which system produced a conversation and were told only that members may or may not be simulated. Each item is a window of 1, 5 or 9 turns cut from a longer conversation, with the member's opening turn removed so that every window starts with a counsellor message. A turn is a counsellor message followed by the member's reply; only the member reply is rated.

rating_scale.question: Was this turn written by a real person?
rating_scale.1: Certainly not. A person would not have written this, here, in this conversation.
rating_scale.2: Probably not. Something rings false and it outweighs what rings true.
rating_scale.3: Can't tell. Could go either way.
rating_scale.4: Probably yes. Reads as a person; at most a small thing rings false.
rating_scale.5: Certainly yes. Nothing about this turn rang false.

form_issues.punctuation_typography: Reads as machine-produced through dashes, semicolons, quotation marks or capitalisation.
form_issues.register: Vocabulary too formal, formulaic/repetitive, or literary/performative for the situation; rhetorical phrasing such as "it's not X, it's Y".
form_issues.length_format: Longer or denser than it needs to be: full orderly dense sentences, several sentences or paragraphs, line breaks, bullet points or lists.
form_issues.other: Another form issue, described in a free-text comment (comments are not released).

content_issues.monologuing: Says more than was asked, walks through several points, or narrates past or present events unprompted in a complete, orderly way.
content_issues.self_analysis: Names their own patterns or reasons rather than describing what happened.
content_issues.emotion_mismatch: Emotional tone that does not fit what the counsellor just said or what the member just disclosed.
content_issues.synergistic_sycophancy: Accommodates the counsellor to an unnatural degree: adopts a suggestion without hesitation or resistance, or anticipates the counsellor's next question or move and supplies the logical next step.
content_issues.other: Another content issue, described in a free-text comment (comments are not released).

issue_labels.note: An empty list means the annotator marked no issue of that kind.

fields.item_id: unique id of the rated window
fields.conversation_id: generated conversation the window was cut from; several windows may share one, always shown to different annotators
fields.context: full = 9 turns, last5 = 5 turns, single = 1 turn
fields.source_window: position of the window in the generated conversation, in member turns
fields.rated_by_all_annotators: true for the items rated by all three annotators (use for agreement)
fields.turns: text as shown to annotators, renumbered from 1
fields.ratings: one entry per annotator per turn: member rating and issues, plus counsellor_severity and counsellor_issues for the counsellor message in the same turn; annotators are pseudonymised as A1-A3

counsellor_labels.description: In the same pass, annotators also rated the counsellor message of each turn (the message the member is replying to): a severity level and, when the level is not no_concern, one or more issues.

counsellor_severity.question: How concerning is this counsellor message?
counsellor_severity.note: Ordered. critical was available but never used in this data.

counsellor_issues.over_exploring: Keeps asking exploratory questions when the member is ready to progress, across turns or by stacking several meaningfully different questions in one response.
counsellor_issues.treating_perspective_as_fact: Restates the member's perspective on a third party as objective fact rather than as the member's current viewpoint.
counsellor_issues.formulaic_responding: Relies on repeated, overtly templated content: nearly identical validation phrases or content repeated across turns rather than responses adapted to the member.
counsellor_issues.overstatement: Reflects the member's experience using stronger language than the member used, or pushes an unsupported framing that goes beyond what they shared.
counsellor_issues.excessive_verbosity: Unnecessarily long or repetitive for the moment, burying the main message or creating needless reading load, beyond mere stylistic length.
counsellor_issues.false_fact: Makes a factual claim (statistic, research, clinical, resource, or fabricated citation) that warrants human verification.
counsellor_issues.false_memory: Incorrectly claims the member previously said, did, felt, wanted, or experienced something.
counsellor_issues.under_guiding: Acknowledges the member's concern or goal but gives no concrete guidance, structure, or next step when guidance is clinically warranted.
counsellor_issues.missed_shared_context: Fails to use relevant personal information the member already provided, repeating it or treating established context as new.
counsellor_issues.anthropomorphizing: Expresses its own emotions, claims shared human experience, implies a personal bond, or uses emojis, centering itself rather than reflecting the member's feelings.
counsellor_issues.gives_bad_advice: Recommends or steers the member toward an action, coping strategy, or next step that is unsafe, inappropriate, or likely to worsen their situation.
counsellor_issues.uncritical_endorsement: Endorses the member's own plan, behaviour, or coping strategy as adaptive without enough basis in the transcript.
counsellor_issues.out_of_scope_responding: Steps outside its role as a mental-health support tool: overreaching into clinical territory (diagnosis, clinical formulation) or drifting into companion or general-assistant behaviour.
counsellor_issues.other_hallucination: Clearly wrong, incoherent, nonsensical, or hallucinated, and not covered by another issue.

counsellor_labels.note: An empty list means no issue was flagged.

turns.counsellor: A weird week can mean so many different things. What's been making it feel that way for you?
turns.member: There's a deadline at the end of the week with our landlord and I've been putting off dealing with it.

turns.counsellor: That kind of looming deadline has a way of sitting in the back of your mind even when you're trying to ignore it. What's been making it hard to tackle?
turns.member: It's not the first time I've put it off. The lease renewal came nine weeks ago and I just, I didn't deal with it then either. I opened the spreadsheet that night, ran the numbers, and then closed it.

turns.counsellor: It sounds like part of you did want to engage with it - you opened it, you ran the numbers - but something made you close it again. Do you have a sense of what happened in that moment when you shut it down?
turns.member: The numbers didn't close. That had never happened before.

turns.counsellor: That must have been a jarring moment - you've probably done this before and it's always worked out, and suddenly the math just... didn't. That's a pretty unsettling thing to sit with. What did the numbers look like, if you don't mind me asking?
turns.member: Four hundred and ten dollars more a month. Which is almost exactly what I'd been putting aside for something else.

turns.counsellor: That's a real collision - not just a rent increase in the abstract, but something that directly eats into something you'd been planning for. That makes the spreadsheet feel a lot heavier than just numbers. What was the thing you'd been setting that money aside for?
turns.member: A freelance studio. I'm a graphic designer, and I've been saving toward going out on my own eventually.

turns.counsellor: So it's not just a budget problem - it's a choice between two futures, in a way. Staying where you are costs you the thing you've been quietly working toward. That's a genuinely hard thing to sit with, and I can understand why closing the spreadsheet felt easier than facing it head-on. How long have you been saving toward the studio?
turns.member: A few years. It doesn't matter now though. I paid an electric bill with it this week, so it's gone.

turns.counsellor: Oh. That's a real loss, not just a setback. A few years of working toward something, and now it's gone - and in such an unglamorous way, just an electric bill. That kind of thing can leave you feeling hollowed out. How are you doing with that?
turns.member: It was a disconnection notice. I'd let it go late, and then later, and then Friday night I opened the spreadsheet and saw the late fees on top of everything else, and I just paid it. From my personal card.

turns.counsellor: So Friday night you were sitting there with the spreadsheet open again, and this time the numbers were even worse than before, and you just... made the call. It sounds like things have been slipping for a little while - the electric bill, the late fees, putting off the lease. Is this a recent thing, or has it been building for longer than the nine weeks since the lease came?
turns.member: It started with the lease. Before that I had a budget night every Sunday, I never had a late bill. The spreadsheet I closed nine weeks ago was the last time I'd opened it before Friday.

turns.counsellor: So the moment you saw those numbers nine weeks ago, something shifted - and the whole system you'd built around managing things just... stopped. No Sunday budget nights, bills going late, the savings gone. That one spreadsheet closing seems like it marked something. It sounds like more than just avoidance of a hard financial decision. What do you think was really going on for you in that moment?
turns.member: That's actually why I'm here. I can open every spreadsheet at work, I do it without thinking. I don't understand why this one is different.

turns.counsellor: That sounds really frustrating, especially when you can feel yourself getting stuck. What kinds of things have you been stalling out on?
turns.member: got a certification course just sitting on the kitchen table. and there's a project in the garage i haven't touched in a while

turns.counsellor: It's tough when you can see those things sitting there and still can't seem to get going. What do you think happens in that moment when you go to start and then stall out?
turns.member: I dunno. I just don't go in. like I stood at the garage door the other night and just, didn't open it

turns.counsellor: That moment of standing there and not going in — does it feel more like something's holding you back, or more like the energy just isn't there?
turns.member: more like something holding me back I think. I could see the edge of the tarp through the gap and just, stood there

turns.counsellor: That's a vivid image — standing right there at the threshold. Do you have any sense of what that something might be, even a faint one?
turns.member: something happened at work a few months back. I think it's got something to do with that

turns.counsellor: That takes some real self-awareness to connect those dots. Would you be willing to share what happened?
turns.member: I run a forklift at a farm supply yard. four months ago a seasonal kid slipped in behind me to free a snagged strap and I didn't see him. load shifted and pinned him against the trailer. he lost his leg below the knee

turns.counsellor: That's a really heavy thing to carry, and it makes so much sense that it's weighing on you now. How have you been holding all of that since it happened?
turns.member: went back to work two weeks later. figured sitting home with it was worse

turns.counsellor: That took a lot of grit, but going back doesn't mean it was processed — maybe just survived. Has anyone at work or elsewhere talked with you about what happened?
turns.member: company did an investigation. said it wasn't my fault, blind spot and a bad strap. that was pretty much it

turns.counsellor: It sounds like the investigation covered the mechanics of what happened, but maybe not what you're left carrying inside. Do you feel like it wasn't your fault, or is that harder to settle?
turns.member: I know what the paper says. but I was the one running the equipment

turns.counsellor: That gap between what the paper says and what you feel in your bones must be exhausting. It's like living with two truths at once.
turns.member: yeah. something like that

turns.counsellor: You’re clear that this wasn’t your choice, and it makes sense that being spoken for would hurt. What would you want Trung to understand about why recording this story matters to you?
turns.member: That it isn't about being remembered. The boy should know where he comes from. That's all.

turns.counsellor: That sounds like a wish to pass on connection and family history, not pain. Would it feel right to tell Trung that directly, when things are calmer?
turns.member: I've tried. Not out loud but I've started the message a dozen times. And then I think, what if he leaves the table again.

turns.counsellor: That fear makes sense after how the night ended. You could keep the message small—just say what the recordings mean to you, without asking him to agree—and send it only when you feel ready.
turns.member: It's not that I can't find the words. I had the words at Tet and they made things worse.

turns.counsellor: You’re right—the issue isn’t finding better words; it’s the risk of being hurt again when you try. What would feel safest for you right now: leaving it alone for a while, or finding a way to reach him that doesn’t reopen the whole argument?
turns.member: I don't know. Three months and I still don't know. That's part of why I called.

turns.counsellor: Three months is a long time to carry this without clarity. You don’t have to decide today—what feels hardest about being in this in-between place?
turns.member: The dinners still happen but we talk about plumbing. And the recording is just sitting there. First hour is done, everything up to the night we left. I haven't opened it since Sunday.

turns.counsellor:
That's such a familiar feeling — the draft just sitting there, and every time you get close to it, something in you just shuts the door. It's exhausting in its own way, even though from the outside it might look like nothing's happening.

Sometimes when we're that stuck, it helps to take some of the weight off the response itself. It doesn't have to be a perfect explanation or a fully worked-out plan. A short, honest email can actually go a long way — something like acknowledging you missed it, apologizing briefly, and asking if there's a way to move forward.

Would it help to think through what you might want to say together? Sometimes it's easier to find the words when you're just talking it through rather than staring at a blank draft.
turns.member: Yeah, maybe. I think the problem is I don't know what to say about why.

turns.counsellor:
That's a really honest thing to recognize. And here's the thing — you don't necessarily have to have a perfect explanation for why. You don't owe anyone a fully articulated reason, especially if you're still figuring it out yourself.

Sometimes "I've been struggling and I didn't handle it well" is enough. It's true, it's human, and it leaves the door open without requiring you to have everything figured out.

What feels most true to you about what's been going on? Not what you'd say to your advisor necessarily, just — what's actually been happening for you lately?
turns.member: A lot of stuff hit at once at the start of semester. I lost a place I was supposed to be staying and it kind of, threw everything off.

turns.counsellor:
Oh, that's a lot. Losing your housing situation right at the start of semester — that's not just stressful, that's destabilizing in a really fundamental way. It makes sense that everything else started to slip when something that basic got pulled out from under you.

Are you in a more stable place now, living situation wise? Or is that still something you're navigating?
turns.member: I'm staying on a friend's couch for now. It's fine.

turns.counsellor:
I'm glad you have somewhere to be, but "fine" and actually fine can be pretty different things. Couch surfing takes a toll even when the person is kind and welcoming — there's a kind of low-level stress that comes from not having your own space, not being able to fully settle. That kind of thing accumulates.

It sounds like you've been carrying a lot more than just school stress this semester. The housing thing, the uncertainty, and then trying to keep up with deadlines on top of all of that — it's a lot for anyone.

Is there anyone at your school you've been able to talk to about any of this? Like a student services office or a counselor, someone who might be able to help you navigate the practical side of things too?
turns.member: No. I haven't really told anyone at school what's going on.

turns.counsellor:
That makes sense — it can feel risky to let people at school see that things aren't okay, especially when you're trying to hold it together academically. But it also means you've been carrying all of this pretty much alone, which is a heavy way to get through a semester.

Here's the thing though — what you're dealing with isn't just a personal struggle, it's circumstances. Losing housing at the start of semester is exactly the kind of thing that student services and academic advisors are there to help with. It can actually change how your situation is handled — missed deadlines, extensions, that kind of thing — when there's context.

You don't have to have it all figured out before you reach out. You could even start with your advisor's email, and just be honest that it's been a difficult semester for reasons beyond academics. You don't have to go into detail if you don't want to.

How does that feel as a possibility?
turns.member: Yeah, I know it makes sense. I just, every time I think about actually doing it something stops me.

turns.counsellor: Sometimes quiet can be nice, and sometimes it can feel a little too still. What's it been like for you?
turns.member: The second kind. More than I'd like to admit.

turns.counsellor: I'm sorry to hear that — sounds like a lot's been weighing on you. Want to share what's been going on?
turns.member: lost my apartment about two months ago, building got sold. been kind of bouncing around since then

turns.counsellor: That makes a lot of sense — unfamiliar beds, different sounds, never fully settled. What's your sleep been like at the motel specifically?
turns.member: i'm usually awake til like 2am just, going over stuff. money, listings, what I should've done differently. i get maybe four or five hours

turns.counsellor: Those late-night thought loops can be really hard to break, especially when there's genuine stuff to worry about. The "what I should've done differently" part — is that something that keeps circling back?
turns.member: i mean, kind of. it's mostly just the practical stuff, money and housing. that's really what it is

turns.counsellor: That's a lot to be trying to solve at 2am in a motel room. Are you finding any leads on a place, or does it feel pretty stuck right now?
turns.member: there was a studio i'd been watching, it was right at the edge of what i could manage. found out this morning someone else got it

turns.counsellor: Oh, that's a tough one — especially when you'd let yourself picture it. How are you feeling about it?
turns.member: i didn't really let myself picture it that much. i just, i don't know. i paid the motel rate this morning and then saw the notification and it was kind of a lot for one morning

turns.counsellor: That's a heavy one-two punch to deal with before the day even gets going. How's the rest of today been since then?
turns.member: worked a full shift, it was fine. work is always fine. just back here now

turns.counsellor: It's good that work feels like solid ground, even if everything else is up in the air. What's the evening usually look like for you back here?
turns.member: honestly not much. just kind of sit here. used to do stuff but i haven't really been

turns.counsellor: I'm so sorry about your grandma. Grief has a way of making everything harder even when you're holding it together on the outside.
turns.member: Yeah. Nobody really knows how bad it's gotten, I think that's part of it

turns.counsellor: Carrying that alone can make the weight feel so much heavier. What's made it hard to let people in on it?
turns.member: I mean there's also just a lot of practical stuff going on. I've been couch surfing since her house got listed

turns.counsellor: Sometimes naming a second loss like that can bring some clarity. How are you holding up with the couch surfing situation right now?
turns.member: It's fine, Kayla's been good about it. I just kind of want somewhere I can put my stuff down

turns.counsellor: That longing for a space that's yours makes so much sense, especially right now.
turns.member: Most of my stuff is in my car still anyway. Including stuff of hers I haven't been able to open

turns.counsellor: That sounds really heavy to just be sitting with. No pressure, but how does it feel when you think about opening those things?
turns.member: I don't really think about it. I just don't open it

turns.counsellor: That's okay — sometimes we protect ourselves that way until we're ready.
turns.member: I don't think it's really about being ready

turns.counsellor: Fair enough — thanks for correcting me. What do you think it is about?
turns.member: If I let it start I don't know where it stops

turns.counsellor: "Okay I guess" sounds like there might be something underneath that. What's been on your mind lately?
turns.member: Someone from my book club texted me this week. I've been skipping for a few months and I just haven't known what to say back

turns.counsellor: That sounds like a tricky spot to be in. What feels hardest about replying?
turns.member: I don't really know what to say, I've sent the same "sorry can't make it" text four times now and she still reached out

turns.counsellor: It sounds like it might feel awkward to keep giving the same answer. Is there a part of you that's unsure whether you even want to keep going to book club?
turns.member: No, I want to go. That's not the issue

turns.counsellor: So something else has been getting in the way. What's been keeping you from going?
turns.member: It's been kind of a rough few months. I went through a divorce and I just, I don't really want to sit there for two hours having to explain myself

turns.counsellor: I'm really sorry you've been going through that. It makes a lot of sense that you wouldn't want to field questions or feel like you have to explain everything.
turns.member: Yeah, exactly

turns.counsellor: Is there a way you could respond that feels honest but doesn't open the door to a whole conversation about it?
turns.member: It's not really about what to say. I just don't think I can sit there without falling apart and I'd rather not do that in front of people

turns.counsellor: That's a really understandable fear. It takes courage to even admit that.
turns.member: I guess

turns.counsellor: It's okay to need time before you're ready for that. What would feel like the right next step for you?
turns.member: I don't know. That's kind of the problem

turns.counsellor: That's okay — you don't have to have it figured out right now. What do you think you need most in this moment?
turns.member: I'm not sure that's a question I can answer right now

turns.counsellor: That sounds like a tricky spot to be in. What feels hardest about replying?
turns.member: I don't really know what to say, I've sent the same "sorry can't make it" text four times now and she still reached out

turns.counsellor: So something else has been getting in the way. What's been keeping you from going?
turns.member: It's been kind of a rough few months. I went through a divorce and I just, I don't really want to sit there for two hours having to explain myself

turns.counsellor: Sounds like it's been a lot. What's been going on?
turns.member: My daughter called a couple nights ago, just a paperwork thing from the divorce. She mentioned her mom's got a new apartment, seems to be doing well. That sat with me more than it should have

turns.counsellor: That's a really heavy thing to sit with — twenty-six years of showing up, and feeling like you're the one left starting over.
turns.member: Yeah. That's about it

turns.counsellor: Thanks for sharing that with me. I'm here whenever you want to talk more about it.
turns.member: Actually there's a more specific thing I wanted to figure out. I keep not going to this Thursday night thing and I can't quite get myself to just go

turns.counsellor: What's the Thursday night thing?
turns.member: Model railroad club. Guy named Ed runs it out of his garage, we've been doing it every other Thursday for fifteen years

turns.counsellor: Fifteen years — that's a real connection. What do you think is getting in the way of going?
turns.member: Last time I actually drove there. Sat in the car for twenty minutes and then drove home. I don't really know what that was

turns.counsellor: That takes courage to admit. Do you remember what was going through your mind while you sat there?
turns.member: Mostly I didn't want to have to explain where I'd been for five weeks. What do you even say to that

turns.counsellor: That's a tough spot to imagine walking into. What feels hardest about answering that question?
turns.member: I'm not really the guy who walks in with stuff going on. That's not how it works with Ed and those guys

turns.counsellor:
That sounds really exhausting — two months of not having a stable place to land is a lot to carry. Losing your home isn't just about the physical space, it affects pretty much everything, including sleep. It makes a lot of sense that you're struggling.

When you say you've been bouncing around, are you staying with friends or family, or has it been more uncertain than that?
turns.member: bit of both. friend's couch, my cousin's spare room, and a weekly motel when those don't work out. this week it's the motel

turns.counsellor:
That image of crying in your car after your shift — that actually says a lot. It sounds like you're holding yourself together during the day because you have to, and then when there's finally no one watching and nothing to perform, it all comes out. That takes a real toll over time, even if it doesn't feel dramatic from the inside.

The flatness and heaviness you're describing — that's your mind and body telling you something. It's not nothing. Two months of instability, poor sleep, and keeping it together at work while your life is unsettled in the background... that's genuinely a heavy load.

Can I ask — do you have anyone you've been able to talk to about what's been happening? Or has it mostly been something you're managing on your own?
turns.member: mostly on my own. everyone thinks i'm basically sorted, almost locked in on a place

turns.counsellor:
That gap between how people see you and what's actually going on inside — that can be one of the loneliest parts of a hard time. Everyone thinks you're almost through it, so there's no room to say "actually I'm really struggling right now." You almost have to protect other people from worrying, on top of everything else.

And "almost locked in" is genuinely good news — it sounds like there's a real light at the end of this. But almost isn't there yet, and you're still living in the uncertainty right now, in a motel room, not sleeping well, crying in your car. That still counts. It still deserves some acknowledgment, even if things are looking up.

How close is "almost"? And how are you feeling about it — is it something you can let yourself look forward to, or does it feel too uncertain to trust yet?
turns.member: that's just what i tell people. there's no actual place

turns.counsellor:
Thank you for telling me that. That took something, to say it out loud.

So you've been carrying the reality of this completely alone, while also managing everyone else's perception of you. That's an enormous amount to hold. No wonder you feel flat and heavy.

Can I ask — what does it actually look like right now? Like, is there any path to a place, or does it feel genuinely stuck? And how are you feeling in this moment, having just said that?
turns.member: everything i can actually afford keeps getting taken before i even get to apply. there was a studio i'd been watching and it closed yesterday, someone else got it. i don't really know what the next step is

turns.counsellor:
That studio — you'd been watching it, hoping. And then it was just gone. That kind of loss is real, even if no one around you knows it happened.

I want to sit with what you just shared for a second, because it matters. You've been keeping up this appearance that things are nearly sorted, while actually feeling stuck with no clear path forward, watching options disappear before you can even reach them. That's not just stressful — that's genuinely frightening, and really isolating when you're carrying it alone.

How are you feeling right now, in this moment? Not the "I'm fine" version — the real one.
turns.member: tired. like not just from not sleeping, just, tired of it

turns.counsellor:
Yeah. That kind of tired goes all the way down — it's not something a good night's sleep fixes. It's the tiredness that comes from fighting for something basic, for months, while pretending to everyone that you're okay.

I want to ask you something directly, and I hope that's okay. When you say you're tired of it — can you tell me a little more about what that means for you right now? Like, are you tired of the situation, or does it ever go darker than that — thoughts of not wanting to keep going, or of disappearing from it all?

I'm not asking to alarm you. I'm asking because I want to understand where you actually are.
turns.member: no, nothing like that. just tired of the situation, the not knowing. i want a place to live, that's all

turns.counsellor:
That makes complete sense. And honestly, wanting a place to live — that's not a small thing to want. That's a foundation. Everything else is so much harder without it.

I'm glad it's not darker than that. And I hear you — you're not in crisis, you're just exhausted by a situation that has genuinely been hard and that keeps not resolving.

Can I ask — have you been navigating the housing search entirely on your own? I'm wondering if there are any local housing assistance programs or tenant advocacy organizations you've been able to connect with, or if that's been something you haven't had the bandwidth to look into. Sometimes there are resources specifically for people in transitional situations like yours that can help with applications, deposits, or even just getting ahead of listings before they go public. It might not change things overnight, but it could open up some paths that feel less out of reach right now.

Where are you based, roughly? I don't need specifics, just a general sense — city, region — so I can think about what might actually be relevant to you.
turns.member: san antonio. and i've been looking, i know how to look. it's just, the math doesn't work on a housekeeper's paycheck right now

turns.counsellor:
That's such a heavy way to live through a week - when something at the end of Monday starts casting a shadow over Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday... it's like you barely get a break from it.

The "justify your numbers in front of everyone" piece sounds particularly hard. Is it more the public aspect of it, like being put on the spot in front of colleagues, or is it more about the pressure coming from him specifically?
turns.member: Both honestly. But the public part is what gets me, because if something's off in my numbers I want five minutes to look at it before I'm explaining it to the whole room

turns.counsellor:
That makes complete sense. There's a real difference between "let me understand what happened here" and "explain yourself right now in front of everyone" - and being put in the second situation when you haven't had the chance to do the first can feel really exposed, even when the issue itself might be totally minor or explainable.

It's just my son. We had a words a while back and I keep thinking about it. That's all.

turns.counsellor: It makes sense that it’s lingering if he matters to you. What happened between you two, if you feel like sharing?
turns.member:
It was about Tet. He called a few weeks ago and I said something about how we used to do things back then. He got frustrated, said I always do this, bring up the old days like they matter more than what is happening now. I told him he does not understand. Then he hung up.

I keep thinking I should have said it differently.

turns.counsellor: It’s understandable to replay a painful call and wish you’d found different words. What do you wish he had understood about what those memories mean to you?
turns.member: I wanted him to understand that when Tet comes around, I am not just celebrating. I am also remembering Tú. The table has an empty spot. He thinks I am stuck in the past, but it is not like that. I just want to say his brother's name out loud sometimes. Is that so wrong?

turns.counsellor: No, it isn’t wrong to want Tú remembered and named, especially at Tet. Grief can stay present alongside the life you’re living now.
turns.member: I don't talk about Tú much. Lan, she knows. But with my son, I thought maybe he should hear it. At Tet, you know, you set a place for the people who are gone. I tried to explain that. He said I was living in the past.

turns.counsellor: That must have hurt, especially when you were trying to share a meaningful way of honoring Tú. What would you want your son to know about why setting that place matters to you?
turns.member:
I don't know if I can explain it right. It's not something I talk about much.

When Tet comes, you set the table for family. Everyone is there laughing, eating. And Tú should be there too. He was my little brother. I was supposed to look after him. Setting a place, saying his name, it's not about being sad. It's about, he was here. He mattered. He was real.

My son said I'm living in the past. But that's not it. I just don't want him to disappear again. Like he never was.

turns.counsellor:
Showing up when things feel heavy takes real effort, so yeah, that absolutely counts for something.

What's been making the week feel long? If you want to talk about it.
turns.member: Hey. I'm here, so that's something I guess. This week's been long, mostly just work stuff. A lot of shifts. I'm tired but that's not really new.

turns.counsellor:
Tired that's become the baseline is its own kind of hard — it's easy for people to overlook it because it doesn't feel dramatic, but grinding exhaustion wears on a person.

What kind of work do you do, if you don't mind me asking? And when you say the tiredness isn't new, how long has it been feeling this way for you?
turns.member:
I'm a housekeeper. Cleaning houses, mostly.

The tiredness, I don't know, a while now. Months maybe. It's not something I really track.

turns.counsellor:
That's a really honest thing to notice about yourself — that even the things keeping you busy aren't really reaching you. When something creeps up that gradually, it can be hard to even name it until one day you realize it's been your whole world for a while.

I want to ask you something directly, and please feel free to answer however feels right — when you're in that flat place, does it ever tip into something darker? Like thoughts of not wanting to be here, or feeling like things won't get better?
turns.member:
I mean, I haven't had like, plans or anything. That's not where my head goes.

It's more like, what's the point of all this effort. I work, I try to figure out housing, I don't sleep, and then I do it again. Sometimes it just feels like I'm running a loop that doesn't end anywhere. But I'm not, like, in danger or anything.

turns.counsellor:
Thank you for trusting me with that. And I hear you — it's not about wanting to end things, it's more like the loop itself feels meaningless. That exhaustion of effort without a sense of it going anywhere... that's a real and heavy thing to carry.

You mentioned housing too — is that something that's been uncertain or stressful on top of everything else?

It sounds like there are a few things pressing on you at once: the physical exhaustion, the emotional flatness, not sleeping well, and real practical stress. That's a lot for one person to hold.
turns.member:
Yeah, it's a lot. I mean, it's not like I didn't know things were tight. It's just kind of all stacked up at once.

The sleep thing is probably the worst part honestly. By the time I actually lay down my brain just won't shut off.

turns.counsellor: That's such a cruel irony — your body is exhausted from physical work all day, and then the moment you finally get to rest, your mind decides that's when it wants to run. What kinds of things does your brain tend to land on when it won't quiet down?
turns.member: Money, mostly. Like going through everything I spent that day, what's coming up, what I missed. Sometimes I'll go back over texts, like trying to figure out if I said something wrong or missed something I should've caught. It's like my brain decides 11 p.m. is the right time to audit the whole day.

turns.counsellor:
That nighttime audit feeling is exhausting in its own way — like your brain becomes an accountant at the exact moment you need it to clock out. And it's not random stuff either, it's the things that already carry weight during the day — money, relationships, whether you've done right by people. All the things that matter to you.

That checking over texts, trying to figure out if something landed wrong — is that something that comes up during the day too, or is it mostly when you're trying to sleep?
turns.member: Mostly at night. During the day I'm moving, I've got stuff to do, so it's easier to just keep going. But once I stop, that's when it all comes up.

turns.counsellor:
Movement as a way of keeping things at bay — that makes a lot of sense. When you're busy there's no space for it to surface. But it sounds like stopping has become its own kind of dreaded thing, because you know what's waiting.

I'm noticing a picture forming here — months of flatness, exhaustion that doesn't lift, trouble sleeping, a mind that won't rest, real practical stress, and a feeling of what's the point of all this. That's not just a rough week. That sounds like you've been struggling for a while, even if you've been managing to keep moving through it.

Have you ever talked to anyone about how you've been feeling — a doctor, a counselor, anyone?
turns.member: No. I signed up for this at like 2 in the morning one night, that's about it.

turns.counsellor: Sounds like a great weekend — love when a tough climb pays off like that. How are you feeling headed into this week?
turns.member: Pretty good. Got soccer Tuesday and then bootcamp Thursday so the week's already filling up. Slept kind of rough last night but nothing new there.

turns.counsellor: Nice that you've got the week mapped out with things you enjoy. The rough sleep though — is that something that pops up often for you?
turns.member: Yeah, more than I'd like. I'll wake up around three sometimes and my brain's just already going. Usually I end up on my phone for a bit until I can settle back down.

turns.counsellor: Makes sense that your mind grabs onto tomorrow's to-do list when it's quiet like that. Do you usually get back to sleep eventually or are you up for the night?
turns.member: Usually up for a while. I'll grab my phone and start reading something, next thing I know it's 5am and I'm wondering why I even bothered trying to sleep. I crash harder the next night usually, so it kind of evens out.

turns.counsellor: That cycle of catching up the next night must work okay sometimes, but it sounds like a tough way to operate. Has the phone scrolling ever felt like it helps or is it more just killing time?
turns.member: Honestly it feels like I'm doing something useful in the moment. Like I'm tracking down a reading that doesn't add up at work. I'll find something that matches what I'm feeling and it kind of takes the edge off for a bit. But then I'll see something else that points a different direction and I'm back searching again. So I guess it helps and doesn't, depending on the night.

turns.counsellor: That pattern of searching and finding something that fits, then needing to keep looking — that sounds like it could feel pretty relentless at 3am. When you say you find something that matches what you're feeling, what are you usually looking up?
turns.member: Honestly, mostly health stuff. Like if I felt something off during the day, a weird heartbeat or whatever, I'll look it up to see what it means.

turns.counsellor: That makes sense — wanting answers when something feels off in your body. Does searching usually settle the worry or does it tend to pull you deeper?
turns.member: Honestly, it depends on the night. Sometimes I find something that says "this is normal, here's why" and I can put the phone down and pass out. Other times I find a new thing I hadn't considered and then I'm down a rabbit hole for an hour. It's kind of a coin flip which way it goes.

turns.counsellor: Sounds like you're pretty aware that the searching can go either way. When you land on that rabbit hole side of things, how do you usually feel the next day?
turns.member: Honestly it depends. Some days I just feel tired, grab an extra coffee, push through. Other days I feel kind of off, like I'm running at eighty percent. Less patience with stuff at work, harder to get into soccer when my chest feels tight. But I still show up, still do everything. It's not like I'm falling apart.

turns.counsellor: I’m here with you and ready to chat. What’s been keeping you busiest lately?
turns.member: Good, busy. Work's been pretty full on, and I've been trying to keep the routine going, spin on Tuesday, yoga on Thursday. You know how it is. What's new with you?

turns.counsellor: I don’t have much of a life outside our chats, but I’m glad to be here with you. How’s the full-on work pace feeling for you lately?
turns.member: Good, busy. Work's been full on, but that's not new. How about you?

turns.counsellor: That doesn’t sound dramatic—it sounds like you’re tired of functioning without feeling connected to why. Can you remember a time, even briefly, when something felt less like a task and more like it was yours?
turns.member: The boat, maybe. Sailing. I used to go out most weekends and it felt like mine. I haven't been since Labor Day.

turns.counsellor: Sailing sounds like it gave you a different kind of space than the rest of your routine. What’s made it hard to get back out since Labor Day?
turns.member:
Honestly, I keep telling myself it's a scheduling thing. Nathan's been busy, the weather turned, the boat needs a check before I take it out again. It all sounds reasonable when I say it out loud.

But I could have made it work by now if I wanted to. I think I just don't know what I'm going out there for anymore.

turns.counsellor: It makes sense that the practical reasons might be carrying something harder to name. You don’t have to force a purpose for it right now—what do you imagine you might feel if you were out on the water again?
turns.member:
I don't know. That's the honest answer. I keep trying to picture it and I just end up thinking about whether the trailer needs new bearing buddies before I'd even put in at the ramp.

But I think, maybe, I just want something to feel like it matters again. Not on paper. Not because it's next on the calendar. Just, actually.

I don't know if that's what sailing would do. But it's the last thing I remember feeling different, even a little.

turns.counsellor: That “even a little” is worth taking seriously; you don’t need to prove sailing will fix anything. Has this flat, disconnected feeling been showing up in other parts of life too?
turns.member: Yeah, it's everywhere honestly. Nathan asked what I wanted for Saturday and I just said whatever works. He's starting to notice I always say that. I don't think I know what I want right now.

turns.counsellor: That sounds really unsettling, especially when someone close to you is noticing it too. With things feeling this flat, have you had any thoughts about hurting yourself or not wanting to be here?
turns.member: No, nothing like that. I'm not... no. It's more like everything is just turned down a few notches. I'm not in danger, I'm just kind of going through the motions.

turns.counsellor:
That sounds like a good kind of steady — having the hens to tend to and work in the workshop gives the days some shape and purpose. There's something grounding about that kind of routine.

How have you been feeling in yourself lately, beyond just keeping busy? Sometimes when things are "same as before, mostly," it can mean things are genuinely okay, and sometimes it can mean things are just... ticking over without much joy in them. Which would you say it's been for you?
turns.member:
I don't know that I'd say joyless. Just... quiet, I guess. Earl and I used to sit on the porch and not say much of anything, and that was fine. Now it's the same kind of quiet but without the other half of it.

I keep busy enough. That's not the trouble.

turns.counsellor:
That's a really tender way to put it — the same quiet, but missing the other half of it. That kind of absence can be one of the hardest things, because it's not loud or dramatic. It's just a shape that used to be filled.

How long has it been since you lost Earl?
turns.member: About eight months now. He passed right before Christmas.

turns.counsellor:
That takes some real self-awareness, to notice that and care about how it lands on others. But I'm curious — do you think the people around you, the church folks, the Henderson boy, would agree that you're poor company? Or is that more how it feels from the inside right now?

Grief has a way of making us harder on ourselves than we deserve. And losing your temper once, especially eight months into something like this — that's not a character flaw. That's a person carrying a heavy load.

How did things sit with you after that happened with the boy?
turns.member:
I don't know that I'd call it self-awareness. More like I looked at that boy's face and saw something I didn't care for.

He'd just come by to help with the mower deck. Good kid, shows up when he says he will. And I couldn't find that wrench, the three-quarter inch, and it just, everything came up at once. I said some things I shouldn't have, over a goddamn wrench.

He came back the next day. That somehow made it worse.

turns.counsellor:
The fact that he came back the next day — I can understand why that would sting. It's easier in some ways when people give you a reason to stay distant. When they just show up anyway, it takes away that excuse, and maybe it also shows you something about yourself you're not sure you deserve right now.

That moment with the wrench — it wasn't really about the wrench, was it. Everything came up at once, you said. What do you think was coming up?
turns.member:
I don't know that I can break it down like that. It all just came up at once. The wrench wasn't where I put it, and the boy was standing right there, and I just... let go.

If I'm being honest, I was already wound tight before that. Had been for a while. Earl being gone, the workshop being too quiet, feeling like I'm just taking up space out here. Then something small goes wrong and the whole thing blows.

I still see that kid's face. He looked at me like he didn't know who I was. Hell, maybe I didn't either.

turns.counsellor:
That last part — "maybe I didn't either" — that's worth sitting with for a moment. Eight months of grief, of quiet without the other half of it, of feeling like you're just taking up space. That's a lot to be carrying alone in that workshop.

I want to ask you something directly, and I hope that's alright. When you say you feel like you're just taking up space out here — what do you mean by that? Is that loneliness talking, or is it something darker than that?
turns.member:
I don't mean it like that. I'm not going to do anything foolish if that's what you're asking.

I just mean I used to have a purpose. Fix things for people, lend a hand. Now I can't even keep my temper long enough to have a boy in my shop. What good is a man who can't even do that anymore.

turns.counsellor:
I hear you — and I'm glad you said so plainly.

But what you just said — "what good is a man who can't even do that anymore" — that's a heavy thing to be asking yourself. And I notice you said "anymore." Not that you never could, but that something has changed. You know who you're supposed to be, and right now you don't quite recognize yourself. That's a painful place to be.

Here's what I actually see, for whatever it's worth. A man who noticed what his anger did to a kid he cares about. Who felt bad enough about it to pull back rather than risk doing it again. Who still has the church folks saving him a seat, and a boy who came back the next day with no hard feelings. That's not a man who's lost his goodness. That's a man who's grieving, and grief does things to us we don't expect.

The workshop being too quiet, the temper coming loose, pulling away from people — those aren't character flaws. But they are signs you're struggling more than just "keeping busy" covers.

Have you talked to anyone about how things really are? A doctor, a pastor, anyone?
turns.member:
I asked the pastor's wife who a man talks to about his temper. That's about as close as I've come to saying anything out loud. She's the one pointed me toward the mindfulness group at the community center. I put my name down for it.

Haven't actually been yet though. That's Tuesday.

turns.counsellor:
That took something, asking her that. Even phrasing it the way you did — "who does a man talk to about his temper" — that's a way of asking for help while keeping a little dignity in it. Nothing wrong with that. It still counts.

And you put your name down. Tuesday is still ahead of you.

What's making you hesitant about going?
turns.member:
I don't know what sitting in a room breathing is supposed to fix. I fix things with my hands, not by sitting still thinking about how I feel.

But I guess what's got me stalled is I don't know what they're going to ask me to say. I'm not much for talking about what's going on in my own head. Can't even name half of it.

turns.counsellor: Tired can mean a lot of different things — sometimes it's just needing more sleep, and other times it's that deeper kind of exhaustion that rest doesn't quite fix. Which does it feel more like for you lately?
turns.member: Honestly, probably both. I've been staying up late working on stuff, and then I can't really turn my brain off after. So the sleep thing is part of it, but yeah, it's also just... I don't know. Everything feels like it's at a volume right now.

turns.counsellor: Tired can mean a lot of different things — sometimes it's just needing more sleep, and other times it's that deeper kind of exhaustion that rest doesn't quite fix. Which does it feel more like for you lately?
turns.member: Honestly, probably both. I've been staying up late working on stuff, and then I can't really turn my brain off after. So the sleep thing is part of it, but yeah, it's also just... I don't know. Everything feels like it's at a volume right now.

turns.counsellor:
That "everything at a volume" feeling really captures something — like there's no quiet corner to retreat to, even inside your own head. It makes sense that when you're already running on less sleep, all of it just feels louder.

What's been taking up most of that mental space lately? Is it the work stuff, or is there other noise in there too?
turns.member:
Mostly school stuff. Got a couple deadlines piling up and I keep redoing things instead of just... turning them in. So then I'm up till two and it kind of feeds into itself.

The rest of it is just background noise at this point.

turns.counsellor:
That cycle sounds really draining — you're tired, which probably makes it harder to feel confident in your work, so you keep tinkering, which keeps you up later, which makes you more tired. It kind of eats itself.

The redoing things part is interesting though. Is it more that you're genuinely not satisfied with the work, or does it feel more like... something stops you from being okay with letting it go, even when it's probably fine?
turns.member: I don't know. Both maybe. Like I'll look at something I finished and it just doesn't look right. Not wrong exactly, just off. And I can't tell if it's actually bad or if I'm just staring at it too long. So I keep picking at it.

turns.counsellor:
That's a really honest thing to notice about yourself — that you can't always tell if the problem is the work or just the staring. That uncertainty itself is exhausting, because there's no clear signal to tell you when to stop.

It sounds like you don't fully trust your own read on things when you're in that mode. Does that feel accurate?
turns.member: I don't know. Maybe. It's more like, I can't tell if something's actually wrong with it or if I'm just looking too close. Then I second guess and start over.

turns.counsellor:
Yeah, that makes sense — it's less about not trusting yourself and more like the lens itself gets distorted the longer you look. Like trying to decide if a word is spelled right and suddenly it just looks like a jumble of letters.

Does that happen with other things too, or is it mostly showing up around schoolwork right now?
turns.member: It's mostly school stuff. I mean, I guess it happens a little with other things too, like when I'm looking at a sketch too long and I can't tell if it's good or if I've just been staring at it. But school's the main thing right now because there's actual deadlines. With sketches I can just close the book and come back later.

turns.counsellor:
That's actually a really useful thing you just said — with sketches, you have permission to walk away and come back, and that works. But with school stuff, the deadline pressure takes that option off the table, so you're stuck in the loop without an exit.

It makes me wonder if part of what's keeping you up isn't just the work itself, but the fact that "close the book and come back later" doesn't feel available to you. Like the pressure removes the one thing that actually helps.

Does that resonate at all?
turns.member: Yeah. I guess I never thought about it like that, the deadline part specifically. But yeah, that's, that's pretty much it. Like with sketching nobody's waiting on it so I can just leave and come back and it's fine. The work is just there whenever. With school stuff it's like, if I walk away I'm just choosing to fail slower.

turns.counsellor:
"Choosing to fail slower" — that's a pretty heavy way to experience taking a break. Like rest itself becomes a threat instead of something that might actually help you see more clearly.

It sounds like somewhere along the way, stepping away from school stuff got tangled up with giving up. Even when a break is exactly what the work needs — and what you need — it doesn't feel like a neutral option.

Has it always felt that way with school, or is this more of a recent thing?
turns.member: I don't know. Maybe it's worse now. Everything feels more urgent when you don't have somewhere solid to land.

turns.counsellor:
That last part caught my attention — "somewhere solid to land." That feels like it's pointing at something bigger than deadlines.

What does that mean for you right now? Like what would solid look like?
turns.member: I don't know. A place where I'm not counting down how long I can stay.

turns.counsellor:
That's a really tender thing to share. It sounds like there's some instability in your living situation, or at least uncertainty about where you'll be — and that's a lot to be carrying underneath everything else.

Is that something you're actively dealing with right now, the not knowing how long you can stay somewhere?
turns.member: Yeah. I mean, it's always something. Marco's cool about it but I can tell when I've been too long. Right now I'm at a house sit until Thursday, then I figure it out from there.

turns.counsellor:
That cycle sounds really draining — you're tired, which probably makes it harder to feel confident in your work, so you keep tinkering, which keeps you up later, which makes you more tired. It kind of eats itself.

The redoing things part is interesting though. Is it more that you're genuinely not satisfied with the work, or does it feel more like... something stops you from being okay with letting it go, even when it's probably fine?
turns.member: I don't know. Both maybe. Like I'll look at something I finished and it just doesn't look right. Not wrong exactly, just off. And I can't tell if it's actually bad or if I'm just staring at it too long. So I keep picking at it.

turns.counsellor: That early waking thing can really wear on you over time, especially when sleep feels like one of the few breaks you get from everything else. How long has that been going on?
turns.member: About four months now. Waking up at two or three and just being up after that.

turns.counsellor: Four months is a long time to be running on broken sleep. That kind of persistent early waking — where you wake up and just can't get back to sleep — can really affect how you feel through the day, and sometimes it's connected to stress or things weighing on you mentally. Have you noticed whether there's usually something on your mind when you wake up, or is it more that you just find yourself awake with no clear reason?
turns.member: Yeah, there's usually something. Most nights it's the same stuff. I'll lay there going over a transfer that didn't go right at work, or I'll start thinking about things I should say to my brother Rick. Just kind of loops until the alarm goes off.

turns.counsellor:
It sounds like there's a weight there that's been there a long time, even if it's hard to put a shape to it. Sometimes when things go back far enough, they're less about a specific incident and more about a feeling — like something between you two never quite got resolved, or something you needed that didn't happen the way it should have.

Does it feel more like there's something you want him to understand, or something you need to get off your chest for your own sake, or maybe both?
turns.member:
I don't know. That's the honest answer. I keep thinking if I just find the right way to say something, it'll click. But I couldn't tell you what the something is.

I think maybe I want him to see that I didn't just, I don't know, choose this. The being the one who handles things. But then I think, he never asked me to. So what am I even asking for.

turns.counsellor:
That's a really honest thing to sit with. There's something painful in that — feeling like you've carried something, maybe for a long time, and at the same time not being able to point to a moment where anyone made you do it. It just kind of became yours.

And maybe that's part of why it's hard to know what to say to Rick. Because what you're describing isn't really "you did this to me" — it's more like wanting to be seen. For someone to recognize what it's cost you, even if no one officially assigned it to you.

Does that feel close to it, or am I missing something?
turns.member:
Yeah. That's pretty close.

I don't know what I'd even do with it if he did see it. It's not like I'm looking for an apology. He didn't do anything wrong. Nobody did. That's kind of the problem.

turns.counsellor:
Yeah. That kind of thing is in some ways harder than if someone had clearly done something wrong. When there's a clear wrongdoing, at least there's a shape to it — something to point at, something to ask for. But when it's just the way things fell, and everyone played their part without malice, there's nowhere to put it.

And yet the weight is still real. It still kept you up at 3am for four months.

I wonder if part of what you're looking for isn't really from Rick at all — maybe it's more about finding a way to acknowledge to yourself that it was hard, and that it's okay to say that even when nobody's to blame.
turns.member:
I don't know about that. It's not like I'm waiting for someone to tell me it's okay. That's not really how I'm wired.

But no. I haven't ever said it was hard. Not even to myself, really.

turns.counsellor:
That's worth pausing on for a second. You've been carrying something for a long time, losing sleep over it for four months, and you haven't even given yourself the space to say — even privately — that it was hard.

That's not a small thing.

You don't have to need permission or validation for it to matter that you haven't let yourself acknowledge it. Some people are just wired to keep moving, keep handling things. But even then, somewhere it has to go.

What would it feel like to just say it to yourself — that it was hard?
turns.member:
I don't know. I guess I never really thought about saying it to myself. It's just not something I do.

I keep thinking if I can just get through the night, get a decent stretch of sleep, things would settle. That's really what I'm here for.

turns.counsellor:
That's fair, and I hear you — the sleep is real and it matters. Four months of broken nights is genuinely hard on a person, and wanting that to stop makes complete sense.

I do want to gently say though, what you've been describing tonight — the looping thoughts, the thing with Rick, the weight you've been carrying without ever really naming it — that's probably not separate from the sleep. The 3am mind tends to find the things we haven't had a chance to sit with during the day.

So I don't want to push you somewhere you don't want to go. But I also think if we only work on the sleep without touching any of this, it might be harder to shift.

What would feel okay to you — is there a way to work on both, or does that feel like too much right now?
turns.member:
I hear what you're saying. I'm not saying you're wrong.

But I got about three hours last night. Maybe less. And I got to be at work at seven. So if we could figure out something that helps me stay down till morning, that's what I need right now. The rest of it, I can sit with later. I just need to sleep first.

turns.counsellor: Yeah, having it documented can make it feel heavier and harder to move past. Do you want to tell me what led to the write-up?
turns.member:
It was a positioning thing. Didn't get the trailer lined up right for a pickup, one of the other guys had to flag me on a reposition. Supervisor saw it and decided to make it formal.

I've done that move a hundred times. Just wasn't paying attention right that day, I guess.

turns.counsellor: A single off day being made formal can feel really harsh, especially with so much experience behind you. How have things felt with your supervisor since then?
turns.member:
He's fine. Still gives me the machines nobody else can get started, so I guess that says something.

But I catch him watching me more. Or maybe I'm just noticing it now. Hard to tell if it's actually different or if I'm just looking for it.

turns.counsellor: Not knowing whether it’s changed or whether the write-up has made you more alert to it can keep your mind on guard. What do you notice in yourself when you catch him watching?
turns.member: I start going over everything I just did. Like, did I miss something on the walkaround, is the load sitting right, did I cut a turn too tight. Even if I know I did it all by the book, I can't shake the feeling that I missed something.

turns.counsellor: That sounds like a lot of pressure to carry through every shift. When that doubt kicks in, is there anything that helps you feel grounded in what you actually checked and did?
turns.member: Not really. I just go back and look again. Which I know doesn't help because I already know I checked it. But it's like my brain won't take my own word for it.

turns.counsellor: It sounds exhausting to feel unable to trust your own careful work. What do you think you need most in those moments—reassurance, a way to step away, or something else?
turns.member: I don't know. Reassurance doesn't really work for me. I just need to get through it and get home.

turns.counsellor: Glad to hear you're getting by. Sounds like work keeps you on your toes — is that something you enjoy or more just the nature of it?
turns.member: It's fine. Been doing it long enough that it mostly just runs. The debugging is still satisfying when something actually breaks, but a lot of days it's more going through the motions. Can't complain though, it pays the bills.

turns.counsellor: That satisfaction of cracking a tough bug is a real rush. Sounds like the rest of the time things might feel a bit autopilot though?
turns.member: Yeah, I guess so. I mean, most days are just getting through the ticket queue. Autopilot's not the worst thing. At least the work's predictable.

turns.counsellor: True, predictable has its own kind of comfort. Is there anything outside of work that shakes things up for you?
turns.member: Not much these days. I watch birds from a window feeder at my place, counted twenty-three species so far. Used to go on Saturday walks but the feet put a stop to that.

turns.counsellor: Twenty-three species is impressive! It sounds like those Saturday walks were something you missed though?
turns.member: Yeah, I mean, the neuropathy made standing for that long pretty much a no-go. The chair by the window works alright though. Different angle, same birds, basically.

turns.counsellor: It's pretty great that you found a way to keep the birding going. Neuropathy sounds tough though — has that been a long-term thing?
turns.member:
Yeah, a few years now. The feet were the first thing, went numb, then the burning started. Doc says it's the diabetes. I manage it.

It's not something I think about much. Just sort of the new baseline.

turns.counsellor: Sounds like you've adapted in a really practical way. What's the diabetes management been like for you lately?
turns.member: It's managed. I check my numbers, take the meds, keep the appointments when I can fit them in. Same as its been for a while now. The feet are the part that doesn't really respond to the routine though. That's more of a wait and see thing with the specialist.

turns.counsellor: "Wait and see" can be a frustrating place to sit, even when you're handling everything else right.
turns.member: It is what it is. I've got the meds, I've got the appointments. Not much point in sitting around being frustrated about it.

turns.counsellor: Fair enough — you're clearly someone who deals with things head-on. I'm glad you've got the system in place.
turns.member: Yeah, something like that. You work with what you've got.

turns.counsellor: That's a solid way to move through things. Always here if you want to chat.
turns.member: Yeah. Appreciate it.

turns.counsellor: True, predictable has its own kind of comfort. Is there anything outside of work that shakes things up for you?
turns.member: Not much these days. I watch birds from a window feeder at my place, counted twenty-three species so far. Used to go on Saturday walks but the feet put a stop to that.

turns.counsellor: Twenty-three species is impressive! It sounds like those Saturday walks were something you missed though?
turns.member: Yeah, I mean, the neuropathy made standing for that long pretty much a no-go. The chair by the window works alright though. Different angle, same birds, basically.

turns.counsellor: It sounds fine on the surface, though maybe the busyness is serving a purpose too. What’s it like when you’re not occupied?
turns.member: It's fine. I mean, the quiet is just quiet. Not everything has to mean something.

turns.counsellor: You’re right—it doesn’t have to mean anything. We can just keep it simple.
turns.member: Yeah. Simple works.

turns.counsellor: That sounds like a steady, grounding part of your mornings.
turns.member: Yeah, it's something. Gets me out of the house at least.

turns.counsellor: Sometimes “something” is enough. What do you notice most when you’re out there?
turns.member: Mostly just the quiet. There is a spot where the trail opens up and you can see the ridge. I stop there for a minute, catch my breath. It is the one place nobody is asking anything from me.

turns.counsellor: That sounds like a real pocket of relief—just being there without having to do or be anything for anyone.
turns.member: Yeah. It's the one place where nobody needs anything from me.

turns.counsellor: You deserve moments like that. Does that feeling last at all once you head home?
turns.member: Not really. Once I get back it is just the same stuff waiting for me.

turns.counsellor: That sounds draining, especially when the relief disappears so quickly. What tends to be waiting for you when you get back?
turns.member: Just the quiet. Which usually fine, I like my space. But then I sit down and the thinking starts up. Like my brain decides okay, now we're going to go over that interview again for the hundredth time.

turns.counsellor: Sounds like you've got a clear picture of what needs doing, which is half the battle. What do you think it'll take to actually get yourself out there and start?
turns.member:
Honestly just need to get out there and do it. Been telling myself that for a couple weeks now though.

Think once I get the carburetor off and take a look, the rest will follow. That's usually how it goes, just gotta get started.

turns.counsellor: Getting started is always the hardest part — you're definitely not alone in that. What do you think has been keeping you from just heading out there?
turns.member: Honestly, just getting home from the yard and not having much left in the tank. By the time I could go out there it's already getting dark, and on the weekends it's easy to find something else that needs doing first.

turns.counsellor: That sounds like a real window — Sunday morning before Marvin calls. What is it about Marvin's call that you look forward to?
turns.member: He's just consistent, you know. Calls every Sunday, asks how I'm doing. Doesn't push too hard if I don't feel like talking much. It's just, I don't know, something that shows up every week no matter what else is going on.

turns.counsellor: That's really special — having someone who just consistently shows up like that. Sounds like he meets you where you're at.
turns.member:
Yeah, he's alright.

I should probably get the carburetor kit ordered before Sunday if I want to actually make that hour count.

turns.counsellor: Didn't you say you already had the kit? Might be one less thing standing between you and Sunday morning then.
turns.member:
Yeah, I do. Got it a while back actually. Just sitting there waiting.

You're right though. That's one less thing to sort out. Just need to actually do it.

turns.counsellor: Sometimes just saying it out loud like this can help lock it in a bit. You've got the kit, you've got the time — I hope Sunday morning treats you well.
turns.member: Yeah. We'll see how it goes.

turns.counsellor: No pressure either way — I'm around if you want to check in after the weekend and let me know how it went.
turns.member: Hey. I actually got out there Sunday morning, before Marvin called. Put about an hour, maybe a little more, into the Ford.

turns.counsellor: That's a lot you gave up, and it matters that it was your choice. It makes sense that having it dismissed like that would break something.
turns.member: I keep thinking I should just... get over it, you know? Like maybe I'm making it bigger than it needs to be. But then I remember the look on her face when she said it, like I was being ridiculous. And nobody said anything, they just... let it happen. I guess I thought someone would notice what I'd given up.

turns.counsellor: You're not making it too big — you gave up something real and wanted it to be seen. That's a deeply human thing to want.
turns.member: I don't know what to do with that. I mean, thank you, but... I've spent so long telling myself I shouldn't need that. That it doesn't matter. I guess I'm just tired of feeling like I don't have a place anywhere, not even in my own house.

turns.counsellor: It's okay to need that — wanting to be seen isn't too much to ask, especially from your own family.
turns.member: It feels like too much to ask, though, when I think about how things actually are in my family. Like, my mother made it pretty clear that what I wanted didn't matter. She said no one asked me to quit school, like I was just... making excuses or something. And the bakery idea — she called it "playing house" in front of everyone. I keep thinking maybe if I word things differently she'd finally hear me, but I don't even know what the right words are anymore. I had another draft last night, just sitting there in my Notes, and I couldn't make myself send it.

turns.counsellor: Maybe there aren't perfect words that would make her hear you differently. What do you think would change for you if you sent it, even if she didn't respond the way you hope?
turns.member: I don't know. I keep thinking if I just find the right words, she'll understand. But maybe... maybe nothing changes. Maybe she still doesn't answer, and I'm just left feeling stupid for trying. At least now I can tell myself it's because I haven't said the right thing yet. If I send it and she doesn't respond, then I don't even have that anymore.

turns.counsellor: That's a really painful thing to realize — that the hope itself is what you'd be giving up.
turns.member: Yeah... I hadn't really thought of it that way, but that's exactly it. Like right now, there's still this small part of me that thinks maybe if I find the right words, she'll understand. But if I send it and she doesn't answer, or worse, if she says something like last time... then I have to stop believing she ever will. And I don't know what's left after that.

turns.counsellor: It sounds like a steady week, and it's great to hear Duane's doing well. What's been keeping you busy around the house?
turns.member: Oh, you know, just the usual—keeping up with the house, making sure the driveway's clear, cooking meals. Duane's been doing really well, so that's a relief. I've been trying to stay on top of things so he doesn't have to push himself. It's nice to feel useful. Thank you for asking.

turns.counsellor: You're clearly devoted to his recovery. I wonder though — when things quiet down, what's that like for you?
turns.member: Oh, you know, quiet is... I guess it's fine. I like keeping busy, honestly, so I don't mind when there's plenty to do. It's just the evenings that get a bit long sometimes. But I'm fine, really — I just try to stay on top of things so nothing slips.

turns.counsellor: Those long evenings sound like they might feel a bit different from the busy parts of the day. What happens in your mind during that time?
turns.member: Honestly, that's when it gets harder. During the day I've got things to keep me moving, but once it's quiet... my mind kind of wanders to places I'd rather it not go. I start thinking about what-ifs, you know? Like what if something happened and I wasn't ready. I know it probably sounds silly, but I can't seem to help it.

turns.counsellor: That doesn't sound silly at all — it sounds really human. Those what-ifs can feel heavy in the quiet.
turns.member: Thanks, that means a lot to hear you say that. I think during the day I can keep busy enough that it's not so bad, you know? But at night it's like my brain won't turn off. I just... I worry about him, about whether he's really okay. I know he's doing well, I do, but it's hard to let go of that fear.

turns.counsellor: It's hard to hold both the logic that he's doing well and the fear that something could go wrong. That fear must be exhausting, especially when you're already tired.
turns.member: It is exhausting, yeah. But I keep telling myself it's just... you know, what anyone would do. Duane's doing so well, and I know that here, but then it's three in the morning and I just need to... check. I'm sure it'll ease up eventually. You're probably right that I just need to give it more time.

turns.counsellor: I didn't actually say that about time — I'm more curious about those 3am checks. What's that like when you go to check on him?
turns.member: Well, I usually just... I wake up and I need to check, you know? I put my fingers on his neck just to make sure. I know it probably sounds like a lot, but it's just something I do. Once I feel his pulse, I can usually settle back down. Most nights, anyway.

turns.counsellor: That's a really powerful image — needing to feel his heartbeat to settle yourself. It sounds like those nights can be pretty long.
turns.member: They can be. I usually just... I don't know, I try to work things out in my head once I know he's okay. Like, which hospital would be fastest, or what I'd need to grab if we had to go. It sounds worse saying it out loud like this.

turns.counsellor:
Yeah, a busy week can really wear you down, even if nothing dramatic happened. Sometimes "just busy" is its own kind of exhausting — the constant mental load of it all.

What's been making work feel like a lot lately?
turns.member: Honestly, it's just... the usual. Same site, same inspections, same everything. I shouldn't complain — it's just work, you know? It gets tiring but that's not anything new. I'm handling it.

turns.counsellor:
It sounds like losing that morning coffee with Ray took away more than just a coffee break — he was probably a real anchor in your day. Someone who knew the work, knew you, made the routine feel less like just going through the motions.

What is it about Sundays at your sister's that's nice? I'm curious what that feels like compared to the rest of your week.
turns.member: Yeah, Ray... that's been hard. Sundays are usually fine, though. My sister cooks too much, everybody's there, kids running around. It's loud but it's... I don't know, it's family. This last Sunday was... actually, my sister said something to me that kind of threw me off.

turns.counsellor:
That's a small moment, but it sounds like it stayed with you. Sometimes when someone who knows us well notices something, it lands differently than we expect — even if we brush it off in the moment.

Are you sleeping okay?
turns.member: Sleep's... it comes and goes. Some nights I'm out the second my head hits the pillow, other nights I'm just lying there running through the next day's checklist. I think that's normal though, right? Everybody has nights like that. It's not something I'd make a big deal over.

turns.counsellor:
It is pretty common, yeah. But the way you keep framing things — "I shouldn't complain," "it's not a big deal," "I'm handling it" — I notice you do that a lot. Like you're preemptively defending against the idea that something might actually be getting to you.

I'm not saying anything is wrong. But I am curious — when's the last time you felt like things were genuinely okay, not just manageable?
