turns.member:
Honestly, I don't know. Ray and I used to have coffee every morning before shift — twenty years of that. He'd tell me about his garden, I'd tell him what was bugging me about the site, and it just... it felt normal. Like I had a place that wasn't just about getting the job done. Since he left for treatment, I guess I've just been going through the motions.I don't... I mean, things are fine. They're manageable. That's not nothing.

I guess... Ray's coffee breaks were something I looked forward to. But that's just coffee, that's not— I don't know. That was probably the last time I felt like I wasn't just getting through the day. I hadn't thought about it like that before.

turns.counsellor:
That's a really honest thing to recognize. Twenty years of morning coffee with someone who actually knew you — that's not "just coffee." That's connection, consistency, someone to process things with. Losing that, even temporarily, is a real loss. It makes sense it's left a gap.

And it sounds like you've been carrying that gap pretty quietly.

How is Ray doing, do you know?
turns.member: He sent a message a couple weeks back. Said the treatment's rough but he's hanging in. I wanted to ask more, but... I don't know, I didn't want him thinking he had to reassure me when he's the one going through it. So I just said he's been missed on site and left it at that. I keep wondering if I should've said more, but I wouldn't know what to say that wouldn't just make it about me.

turns.counsellor:
That says a lot about you — that even when you're missing him, your first instinct is to protect him from having to take care of you. That's a kind impulse. But it also means you ended up holding all of it alone.

You don't have to make it about you to let someone know they matter to you. "I've been thinking about you" isn't the same as asking him to carry your feelings.

But I'm also noticing — it sounds like you're pretty practiced at not wanting to be a burden. Is that something that shows up in other parts of your life too?
turns.member: I mean, that's just... yeah. I guess I learned early on that people have their own stuff going on. You don't want to add to it. My mom always said, "be the one who brings the casserole, not the one who needs it." So that's... I don't know, that's just how I operate. At work, at family stuff, everywhere really. You keep things running, keep it light, and nobody has to worry about you. It's not a burden thing, it's just... easier for everyone that way.

turns.counsellor:
That's a really clear picture of how you learned to move through the world. And it probably has served you well in a lot of ways — you sound like someone people can rely on, someone who shows up.

But I want to gently reflect something back to you. You're sitting here, a little worn down, missing your friend, not sleeping great, going through the motions — and your instinct is still to frame it as "not a big deal" and make sure nobody has to worry about you. Including, maybe, yourself.

Who brings you the casserole?
turns.member: Nobody. I mean, my sister brings food sometimes, but that's just what she does for everybody. After the divorce I figured out you handle things yourself, and that worked fine. I don't need somebody to — I'm not sitting around waiting for that. I just keep going.

turns.counsellor: It sounds like you’ve had plenty to keep your hands busy. How have you been feeling when things get quiet?
turns.member: Things are fine. When it gets quiet, I just... find something to do with my hands. The garden mostly, or dishes. There is always something to keep busy. It is when I stop that the... it is harder to settle, yes.

turns.counsellor: It sounds like stillness brings up something difficult. What tends to show up for you in those moments?
turns.member: The memories. Things I thought I had... put away. At night, mostly, or when I am alone in the kitchen. The water running, a smell, and then I am somewhere else. I try to tell myself it is finished, that it is all behind us. But lately it does not feel finished.

turns.counsellor: That sounds unsettling, especially when ordinary moments suddenly pull you back. Would it feel okay to share a little about what those memories are connected to?
turns.member: I... it is hard to say it out loud. Some of it goes back a long way, to when we left Vietnam. I started writing it down for my grandchildren, to have the record. But my son Trung, he... he said something at Tet that I cannot stop hearing. I thought I was doing something good, but maybe I was only opening something that should have stayed closed.

turns.counsellor: Writing for your grandchildren sounds like it came from care, and it makes sense that Trung’s response has stayed with you. What did he say at Tet?
turns.member: He said he would hand a child his nightmares just to be remembered. That he didn't understand why I would want to pass any of it forward. Then he drove off before midnight, and we have not really talked since. I keep thinking I should have just kept the story where it was, quietly, and none of this would have happened.

turns.counsellor: That was a painful thing to hear from your son, especially when your intention was to leave something meaningful. Do you feel more pulled to reach out to him, or to put the writing aside for now?
turns.member: I keep thinking I should call him, but then I imagine sitting across from him and I cannot find the right words. Every sentence I practice sounds wrong before I even pick up the phone. So I put it aside and go work in the garden instead. The writing is sitting where I left it that night. I have not opened it since.

turns.counsellor: It makes sense that the call feels heavy when you’re carrying both hurt and uncertainty. You don’t have to find perfect words before reaching out—what might you want him to understand most?
turns.member: I think... I would want him to know that I wasn't trying to hand him anything heavy. I just thought they should know — where the family came from, what Tú never got to see. But maybe he is right. Maybe some things should stay where they are. I don't know anymore what is remembering and what is just... pulling up things that were better left quiet.

turns.counsellor: There may be room for both: honoring what was lost and being careful about how much others are asked to carry. What do you feel Tú’s story means to you?
turns.member: He was... he was the youngest, you know. He had his whole life coming, and he waited so I could go first with my wife and son. I was the older brother, I should have been the one to wait. Every year I have is... I don't know how to say it. It feels like something that should have been his.

turns.counsellor: Losing Tú that way sounds like a grief you’ve carried for a very long time, and I’m glad you said it here. When you feel that your years should have been his, do you ever find yourself wishing you weren’t alive?
turns.member: No, no, nothing like that. It is more that... I feel I am living hours that were his. That I should carry what happened quietly, because at least I am here. There is a shame in that, you understand? Like I took something that was not mine to take.

turns.counsellor: I hear the shame and the weight of surviving, even though you didn’t choose what happened. You didn’t take Tú’s life from him; you were both caught in something painful.
turns.member: I know that here, in this room, what you say is true. I tell myself the same thing sometimes, that I did not choose the sea or the war or any of it. But knowing it here does not change what I feel here. Every year that passes is a year Tú does not get, and I cannot make that right by living well. I have tried to live well for him, for my family, but the guilt... it does not listen to reason. It just sits with me, especially at night, especially when I am alone.

turns.counsellor: It sounds like you’ve had plenty to keep your hands busy. How have you been feeling when things get quiet?
turns.member: Things are fine. When it gets quiet, I just... find something to do with my hands. The garden mostly, or dishes. There is always something to keep busy. It is when I stop that the... it is harder to settle, yes.

turns.counsellor: That sounds unsettling, especially when ordinary moments suddenly pull you back. Would it feel okay to share a little about what those memories are connected to?
turns.member: I... it is hard to say it out loud. Some of it goes back a long way, to when we left Vietnam. I started writing it down for my grandchildren, to have the record. But my son Trung, he... he said something at Tet that I cannot stop hearing. I thought I was doing something good, but maybe I was only opening something that should have stayed closed.

turns.counsellor: Giving it a shot can be a meaningful step, even if things feel mostly manageable. What has Denise been noticing that worries her?
turns.member: Honestly, I think she's just being sweet. She mentioned something about me staying up late, but I told her I've just got a lot on my mind with work and everything. You know how it is — she cares, so she notices things. I appreciate that about her, truly. But I keep telling her, I'm fine.

turns.counsellor:
That image of "one long night that doesn't end" really says a lot. The exhaustion, the uncertainty, the sense that there's no clear way out yet - that's a heavy thing to carry.

The gap between telling yourself "this is temporary" and then opening up listings and seeing those prices... that moment must be really demoralizing. Like the reassurance you're trying to give yourself keeps running into a hard wall.

How are you holding up otherwise - eating okay, getting outside at all?
turns.member: I'm managing. I grab food when I can, usually something from the gas station or whatever's cheap. I don't really go outside unless I'm checking on my car or driving to work. Honestly, I'm fine - it's not like I'm falling apart or anything. I just need to find a place and then everything else will sort itself out.

turns.counsellor: That sounds really exhausting — like the numbers take over before your day even gets started. What do you think would happen if you didn't check?
turns.member: Honestly? I don't know, and that's what scares me. My dad probably didn't check anything, and look what happened to him — dead at forty-nine, just like that. If I don't stay on top of the numbers, something could slip through the cracks and I wouldn't know until it's too late. I know it sounds... I don't know, obsessive maybe. But not checking feels like giving up control, and I can't do that.

turns.counsellor: Losing your dad that young must have left a huge mark on you. It makes sense that you'd want to do everything differently. How old are you now, if you don't mind me asking?
turns.member: I'm thirty-four. So I've got fifteen years left before... before I hit the age where Dad... yeah. Fifteen years. I know it sounds irrational when I say it out loud like that, but I can't help it. Every birthday I think, "that's one less year between me and forty-nine." My roommate tells me I'm being morbid, but he didn't watch his dad drop dead at forty-nine with the same build I've got.

turns.counsellor: I'm glad you're bringing it up here — that takes courage, especially when you learned to just carry things alone. What's it like to say some of this out loud?
turns.member: It's... weird, honestly. I don't think I've ever really said any of this out loud before. In my family, after Dad died, we just... didn't talk about it. Mom kept going, I kept going, and that was that. But sitting here saying it, there's this strange feeling, like I've been holding my breath for years and just let a little bit out. I keep wondering if I'm being dramatic, though. Like maybe I should just handle this on my own like I always have.

turns.counsellor: You're not being dramatic — you're putting words to something you've been carrying silently since you were a kid. That "letting a little breath out" feeling sounds important. What do you make of it?
turns.member: I don't know... it's strange, honestly. I've spent so long keeping all of this locked up tight, just measuring and tracking things on my own, that saying it out loud feels almost wrong. Like I'm breaking some unspoken rule my whole family always followed. But at the same time, I can feel my shoulders dropping a little, like my body knows it's okay to set something down for a minute. I guess I just never realized how heavy it's been, carrying all this monitoring and worrying by myself.

turns.counsellor: Your body is telling you something important right now. What would it feel like to set something down for a little longer than a minute?
turns.member: I don't know... honestly, even the thought of it makes my chest tighten up a little. It's like if I'm not watching the numbers, who's watching them, you know? My dad probably had no idea anything was wrong until one day he was just gone. I know rationally that checking my pressure six times a day isn't going to change some outcome, but it's the only thing I can actually do. Letting it go, even for an afternoon, feels like closing my eyes in the middle of a busy street and just hoping nothing hits me.

turns.counsellor: That image of closing your eyes on a busy street — I can really feel how dangerous that feels to you. You're not just tracking numbers, you're trying to stay alive in a way your dad couldn't.
turns.member: I... yeah. I think that's it. I've never said it like that, but that's exactly what it is. I check the numbers because maybe if I catch something early enough, I can change how the story ends. My dad didn't have that chance — he just... went. And nobody in my family ever talked about it after, like if we didn't say it out loud, maybe it didn't fully happen. But I've been counting the years the whole time, and now that I'm getting closer... it's like I'm trying to outrun something I can't even name. I just want to make it past forty-nine. That's all I want.

turns.counsellor: That's a powerful thing to name — wanting to make it past forty-nine. You're honoring your dad by fighting to live, even if the way you're fighting right now is also wearing you down.
turns.member: I never thought about it like that, that I'm honoring him. I always just... I always thought I was trying not to be him. Like, if I just watch the numbers close enough, I can make sure I don't end up where he did. But maybe... maybe that's the same thing, isn't it? I don't know, it's just strange hearing someone say it out loud when I've never even said it to myself.

turns.counsellor: I’m glad you’ve been mostly keeping up. I don’t have a day of my own, but I’m here with you—what’s the busy pace been like for you lately?
turns.member: Honestly, it's been... a lot, I guess. Work has been pretty intense since I'm still covering both sites, so the days just kind of blur together. Nathan and I had dinner on Wednesday, and I keep thinking about how I didn't really have much to say when he asked about things. I mean, I said I was good, busy — which is true. But there was this moment where he was just looking at me like he wanted more, and I... I changed the subject to his week instead.

turns.counsellor: That sounds like a lot to carry, especially when your days are running together. What do you think made it hard to stay with his question in that moment?
turns.member: I don't know. He asked something simple, I think it was about what I actually want, and I just... nothing came. Like the screen went blank. I changed the subject pretty fast, asked him something about his week instead. It felt safer that way.

turns.counsellor: That sounds frightening and lonely. When you say you feel like you’re disappearing, is it more like feeling numb or unreal, or are you having thoughts of hurting yourself?
turns.member: No, nothing like that. I'm not... I'm not going to hurt myself. It's more like... you know when you open a file expecting it to be full and it's just empty? That kind of unreal. Like I've been the spreadsheet and the calendar and the person who handles things, and underneath all that there might not be anything solid. I keep waiting for something to surface, some answer about what I actually want, and it's just quiet. That quiet scares me more than anything else would.

turns.counsellor: That empty feeling sounds scary, especially when you’ve had to stay in “handle things” mode for so long. You don’t have to force an answer right now; it may be enough to notice that the quiet is there and that you’re not alone with it.
turns.member: Thanks. That's... I mean, part of me wants to ask what the assignment is, like there should be a spreadsheet for this too. I did actually get up at one in the morning the other night to add a row to this options spreadsheet I've been keeping about different directions I could go. Nathan asked me something at dinner on Wednesday and I couldn't answer him, and then I just kept replaying it in my head until I couldn't stand it. So I got up and added another row, like if I just had enough columns the answer would show up.

turns.counsellor: It makes sense that structure feels reassuring when the answer feels out of reach. What does adding another row give you in that moment—relief, a sense of control, or something else?
turns.member: It's... I don't know, it's like if I can make it a row with columns and weights, then it's a problem I'm solving instead of a question I can't answer. Like I'm doing something about it, even if I'm not actually getting closer to an answer. I guess it feels like control, for a few minutes anyway. Like there's a version of me that's still working, even at one in the morning. And then I can close the laptop and feel like I handled it, even though nothing actually got decided.

turns.counsellor: That makes a lot of sense—solving a defined problem can offer a brief foothold when uncertainty feels exposed. What do you notice in yourself after that relief fades?
turns.member: Honestly? It's like the relief didn't even happen. I close the laptop and I'm right back where I started, except now it's one-thirty in the morning and I'm tired on top of everything else. The question is still there, I just... I've moved columns around it. And then I start thinking maybe I should've weighted the criteria differently, or added something I missed, and that just... it keeps going. It's like I can't get ahead of it.

turns.counsellor: That sounds exhausting—the spreadsheet gives the uncertainty somewhere to go, but it doesn’t get to rest. When the loop starts at night, what helps you step away even a little, if anything?
turns.member: Honestly, not much. Sometimes I just get tired enough that I fall asleep, or I'll put on a podcast something about productivity or a news show just to have a voice in the room. I know that's not really stepping away, it's more like drowning it out. The loop just runs until it runs out of gas, I guess. I've never been good at just letting a question sit there unanswered overnight.

turns.counsellor:
That doesn't sound foolish at all. Sometimes we end up somewhere and the thing we came to do just... doesn't happen. The sitting was probably doing something for you, even if it didn't look like much from the outside.

What was going through your mind while you were out there?
turns.member: I was just thinking about Earl, I guess. Forty years of Saturdays we sat out there on that river, and now I'm sitting there alone like an idiot. Didn't even take the rod out — just sat there like something was gonna happen, but nothing did.

turns.counsellor:
Seven months isn't very long, even when it feels like forever. Grief has a way of stretching and compressing time in ways that don't make much sense.

Can I ask — was Earl a close friend, or family?
turns.member: Fishing partner. Forty years of Saturdays out on the Osage. He wasn't family, but... well, I guess you could say he was, in the way that counts.

turns.counsellor:
That last one — the wrench — it sounds like it scared you a little. Like something came out that you didn't expect.

That kind of anger, when it shows up sideways like that — at clerks, at kids, at garage walls — it's often grief that doesn't have anywhere else to go. You're carrying something heavy and it's got to come out somehow, and sometimes it comes out wrong.

But it sounds like you're paying attention. You noticed it wasn't like you. You're here talking about it. That matters.

Have you had anyone to talk to through all this? Family, friends — anyone who knew Earl, or just knows you?
turns.member: Earl was it. We didn't talk much about feelings or any of that, but he was there, and now he's not. I mentioned it to the pastor's wife once, just asked her who a man talks to about... losing his temper and such. She's the one pointed me here.

turns.counsellor:
I'm glad she did, and I'm glad you followed through on it. That took something — to ask her that question, and then to actually show up here. That's not nothing.

It sounds like Earl being there, even without a lot of words between you, was its own kind of steadiness. And now that steadiness is gone, and you're carrying all of it alone. The grief, the anger, the silence. That's a lot for one person.

I want to ask you something directly, and I hope that's okay. The wrench through the wall, the anger that's been spilling out — are you doing okay in terms of your own safety? I just want to make sure I understand the full picture of how you're doing.
turns.member: I ain't looking to hurt myself, if that's what you're asking. I threw a wrench at drywall, not at a person. But I see what you're getting at, and no — I don't like that it's been me lately. That boy's face when I hollered at him... that's what sent me to Donna. I don't want to be the man who makes a kid look like that.

turns.counsellor:
That right there tells me a lot about who you are. The fact that a child's face stayed with you — that it bothered you enough to do something about it — that's not the profile of a man who's lost himself. That's a man who still knows who he wants to be.

You said "I don't want to be the man who makes a kid look like that." It sounds like you've got a pretty clear sense of the man you do want to be. Has that always been important to you — how you carry yourself, how you treat people?
turns.member: I mean... you just do right. You don't think about it like it's something special. On the farm, you fix what's broke, you don't take it out on people, you keep your word. That's just how it's done.

turns.counsellor:
That's a solid way to live. And it sounds like it's been the backbone of who you are for a long time — not a philosophy you talk about, just something you do.

And right now, grief has got into the machinery. Things that used to run smooth aren't running the way they should, and that bothers you. Not because you're worried about your reputation or how you look — but because it's not right. It's not how it's done.

The trouble is, "fix what's broke" is harder when what's broke is on the inside. You can't just replace a part or tighten a bolt. And I think that's part of what's frustrating you — you're a man who knows how to handle things, and this one isn't handling easy.

Does that land close to the truth?
turns.member: Yeah. That's... yeah. That's about the size of it. I can take apart an engine blindfolded and put it back running right, but this... I don't even know where to start. I can't get a socket wrench on it, can't torque it down and call it fixed. And that... that just makes the pressure worse.

turns.counsellor:
Yeah. And grief doesn't come with a manual, and there's no diagnostic code you can pull to tell you what's wrong and what needs replacing. It just sits there, heavy, and the more you try to get a handle on it the more it slips.

But here's what I'd offer — you already did something today that took more guts than most people give it credit for. You talked about Earl. You talked about the river. You told me about the wrench and the kid's face and what Donna said. You named it. That's not nothing, even if it doesn't feel like progress.

You don't have to fix grief like an engine. But you might have to sit with it for a while, the way you sat in that truck Saturday morning. Maybe that's not so different from what you already know how to do.

I'd like to keep talking with you, if you're open to it. Not to fix anything — just to give this somewhere to go besides garage walls. Would you be willing to come back?
turns.member: I don't know that I'd call it guts. Just... didn't know what else to do with it all. But yeah, I s'pose I could come back. Don't got anywhere else to be on Saturday mornings no more.

turns.counsellor:
Hey, I'm glad you're here. "It's been a week" says a lot — sometimes that's all there is to say about it.

What's been weighing on you most?
turns.member: Hey. I don't know, I'm here. It's been... a week, I guess. Nothing too crazy.

turns.counsellor:
Yeah, sometimes a week just accumulates — not one big thing, just everything kind of piling up quietly.

What's it been like for you lately, day to day?
turns.member: Honestly, it's just been... a lot of small stuff. Deadlines and moving around, you know. I'm staying on Marco's couch right now, so that's something. The design files keep stacking up and I just... I don't know. I'll figure it out.

turns.counsellor:
That's a lot to carry — deadlines, being between places, living out of someone else's space. Even when none of it feels "big enough" to complain about, it still takes a toll.

How long have you been at Marco's?
turns.member: A couple weeks, maybe. I don't know, I lose track. Marco's cool about it, he doesn't ask much.

turns.counsellor:
A couple of weeks on a couch, losing track of time — that kind of uncertainty has a way of wearing on you even when you're not consciously thinking about it. It sounds like you're in a bit of a in-between place right now, not just physically.

Is there a plan taking shape, or does it still feel pretty open-ended?
turns.member: It's pretty open-ended. Marco hasn't said anything about me needing to leave, so I just... try not to make it a thing. I keep my stuff packed and stay out of the way as much as I can.

turns.counsellor:
That image of keeping your stuff packed and staying out of the way — that's exhausting in a quiet kind of way. Like you're constantly trying to take up as little space as possible, even in a place where you're supposed to be resting.

How are you sleeping?
turns.member: Sleep's... not great. I keep odd hours anyway, so it doesn't really matter.

turns.counsellor:
It does matter, even if it doesn't feel like it right now. Poor sleep has a way of making everything else harder to manage — the deadlines, the uncertainty, all of it.

When you say odd hours, what does that usually look like for you?
turns.member: I don't really sleep straight through. Sometimes I'm up at 3 or 4 and just... can't get back. If the surf's decent at first light I'll go out for a bit, that helps quiet things down.

turns.counsellor:
That's good that you have something like surfing — something that actually gives your mind a break. Those early morning sessions sound like they might be one of the few times things feel a bit clearer.

What's going on at 3 or 4am when you're lying awake? Is your mind busy, or is it more just... not being able to switch off?
turns.member: Mostly just... thinking about what's due. What I haven't finished. Sometimes I'll open my laptop and just stare at the files. Other times it's stuff like where I'm gonna be next month. It's not like racing thoughts, it's more like a low hum that won't shut off.

turns.counsellor:
That low hum description is really apt — it's almost harder to deal with than racing thoughts because it's not dramatic enough to feel like a "real" problem, but it's always there, quietly draining you.

Work stuff and housing uncertainty all mixing together in the middle of the night — that's a lot for your mind to be holding. Do you feel like you have much of a break from it during the day, or does it follow you around?
turns.member: Surfing helps for a few hours after. Then it's back to the same stuff — laptop open, trying to catch up on design files that should've been done a week ago. I mostly just keep my head down and try not to be in the way.

turns.counsellor:
That phrase again — "try not to be in the way." You've said it a couple of times now. I notice that.

It sounds like you're working pretty hard to be invisible, both at Marco's and maybe in general. Like you're trying to shrink down and just get through things without being a burden to anyone.

Does that feel accurate?
turns.member: Yeah, I guess. I mean, I don't think about it like that. It's just... easier. For everyone.

turns.counsellor:
Hey, I'm glad you're here. "It's been a week" says a lot — sometimes that's all there is to say about it.

What's been weighing on you most?
turns.member: Hey. I don't know, I'm here. It's been... a week, I guess. Nothing too crazy.

turns.counsellor:
Yeah, sometimes a week just accumulates — not one big thing, just everything kind of piling up quietly.

What's it been like for you lately, day to day?
turns.member: Honestly, it's just been... a lot of small stuff. Deadlines and moving around, you know. I'm staying on Marco's couch right now, so that's something. The design files keep stacking up and I just... I don't know. I'll figure it out.

turns.counsellor:
That's a really deep groove to be in — "you just handle it." And it sounds like that groove was carved pretty early, when you were just a kid yourself, taking care of others before you really had a chance to just be taken care of.

I'm curious about something. That ten-year-old who stepped up — did anyone ever check in on *them*? Or was handling it just... expected, and that was that?

Because I wonder if part of what makes it hard to call Rick isn't really about Rick at all. It's that asking for help feels like it means something about you — like it would mean the story you've told yourself your whole life, about being the one who handles things, isn't true anymore. And that story has probably kept you going through a lot.

It's just worth asking: is that story still serving you? Or is it costing you something now?
turns.member: I mean... nobody really asked, but that's just how it was. Mom and Dad were working doubles, somebody had to make sure the little ones ate and got to bed. You don't really think about it like a ten-year-old needing checking on — you just... do what's in front of you. And I guess you're right that it feels strange to even think about asking Rick, like I'd be... I don't know, admitting something I'm not supposed to admit. But it's not that simple — he's got his own family, his own stuff, and I figure if I can just get through this stretch, it'll settle down.

turns.counsellor:
"If I can just get through this stretch" — I hear that. But I want to sit with something you said for a moment, because it caught my attention. You said asking Rick would feel like admitting something you're not supposed to admit. What do you think that something is?

I ask because I notice you've said a few times now that Rick has his own stuff, his own family — and all of that is true. But it also works really well as a reason not to ask. And I wonder if the real barrier isn't Rick's availability at all, but something closer to home. Something about what it would mean about you.

And that ten-year-old who just did what was in front of them, who nobody checked in on — I don't think they disappeared. I think they grew up and kept doing what was in front of them, and got very good at it. But nobody ever told them it was okay to need something too.

You don't have to have this all figured out right now. But I'm wondering — what would it feel like, just hypothetically, to call Rick and say "I need a weekend"? Not whether you would. Just what it would feel like.
turns.member: I don't know. I guess... it would feel like saying I can't do it. Like I'm the one who's supposed to hold everything together, and if I say I need something, then... I don't know, it's like the whole thing cracks. I get that you're saying maybe it's okay to need something, but that's just not how it works, not in my head. It's like there's this rule I can't quite see, but I know it's there. And calling Rick would mean breaking it.

turns.counsellor:
That rule you can't quite see but know is there — that's a really important thing you just named. And I don't think you're wrong that it's real. It's just that rules like that usually get written a long time ago, by circumstances that made them necessary. A household where both parents worked doubles, where someone had to hold things together or things fell apart. That rule probably saved you, in a way. It gave you a role, a purpose, a way to make sense of a situation that was a lot for a kid to carry.

But here's the thing about rules written that long ago — they don't automatically update when the circumstances change. They just keep running quietly in the background, shaping what feels possible and what doesn't.

You're not ten anymore. And the cost of that rule is showing up in your sleep, in your body, in the fact that you're lying awake at 3am turning over a near-miss that scared you. The rule is still protecting something — but it might also be keeping you from something you actually need.

I'm not going to tell you to call Rick tomorrow. But I am curious — if that rule didn't exist, if there was no "supposed to," what would you actually want right now?
turns.member: I don't... I don't know. That's the honest answer. I've spent so long just doing what's next that I'm not sure I know what I want, separate from what needs doing. I guess... sleep. Real sleep, where I'm not listening for her. And maybe not being the only one who knows where everything is and how it all works. But saying that out loud feels... I don't know. Selfish, maybe. Like I'm saying it's too much when other people have it worse.

turns.counsellor:
You just named two real, specific things you want — sleep without vigilance, and not carrying all the knowledge alone. That's not selfish. That's someone who's been running on empty telling the truth about it, maybe for the first time in a while.

And I want to say something about the "other people have it worse" thought, because I hear it a lot, and it's worth looking at directly. It's true that other people have it worse. It's also true that you're exhausted and running on broken sleep and carrying this largely alone. Both of those things are true at the same time. Someone else's harder situation doesn't make yours easier, or less real, or less worthy of care.

That comparison — it's another way the rule shows up, isn't it? Another reason not to need anything.

What strikes me is that you said saying those things out loud feels selfish. But you said them. And the world didn't crack. You're still here, still the person who takes care of your mom, still the one who shows up. Needing sleep and needing help didn't take that away.

I'm wondering — is there any part of you, even a small part, that felt something like relief just now, saying it out loud?
turns.member: Yeah. Maybe a little. It's... I don't know, it's strange. Like saying it out loud makes it real in a way I can't take back, and that's... I don't know if that's good or scary. But I guess... yeah, there's something. Like maybe just a little crack in the wall where some air got in. Doesn't mean I'm going to go call Rick tomorrow or anything. But... I don't know. It's like for a second I wasn't the only person who knew how tired I am.

turns.counsellor:
That crack in the wall, that little bit of air — that matters. You don't have to do anything with it right now. You don't have to call Rick, you don't have to change anything tomorrow. But something shifted just now, and that's real.

And what you just said — "for a second I wasn't the only person who knew how tired I am." I want you to sit with that for a moment, because that's not a small thing. You've been carrying this tiredness alone, probably for a long time. Maybe it's felt safer that way, or just inevitable. But you let someone else see it just now, and you're still okay.

That ten-year-old who learned to just handle it — I don't think they ever got to say out loud how tired they were either. Maybe this is a little bit for them too.

You don't have to have any of this figured out. But I'm glad you said it. And I'm glad there's a little air coming through.
turns.member: Yeah... I don't know what to do with that, exactly. But I guess I don't have to figure it out tonight. I just... thanks for not making me feel like I was being ridiculous. I should probably let Denise know I'll be up for a while — she worries if she wakes up and I'm not in bed. Same time next week?

turns.counsellor:
Same time next week. And no — nothing you said tonight was ridiculous. Not one bit of it.

Go let Denise know you're okay. And I hope tonight you get a little more sleep than last night.
turns.member: Thanks. I'll... yeah, I'll tell Denise I'm okay. She probably already knows I'm not, but she'll appreciate hearing it anyway. I'll see you next week. And thanks for not making me feel stupid about all this.

turns.counsellor:
You're not stupid, and none of this is stupid. It's just a life that's been a lot to carry, for a long time.

Take care of yourself tonight. See you next week.
turns.member: Thanks. I appreciate you saying that. I'll... I'll think about what we talked about. With the drill stuff and all. Maybe I'll try leaving the checklist in the garage tonight. See what happens. See you next week.

turns.counsellor: Hi Alice. When you say “same as usual,” what has that been like lately?
turns.member: Same as usual, I suppose. Just... getting by. Nothing much to report, really.

turns.counsellor: The garage sounds like a small place to breathe. When your mind gets going at night, what tends to be on it?
turns.member: Work, mostly. Just... running through the day, checking things over in my head. Making sure I didn't miss anything. It's nothing.

turns.counsellor: Even if it feels like “nothing,” it sounds draining to keep checking after the day is over. What feels at stake if something gets missed?
turns.member: If something gets missed, it's on me. I signed the entries, so it's my name on it. They've already put me on notice once, so... I don't know. Just trying to make sure nothing slips through, I guess.

turns.counsellor: That makes the pressure feel much more real, not like overthinking. What happened when they put you on notice?
turns.member: Twenty-two years without a mark on my record, and now they hand me a written warning like I'm some rookie who doesn't know the job. New management came in with their logging and audit systems, and suddenly paperwork I never had time for is the thing that can end me. They said it's "performance improvement," but everyone knows what that means. I've seen good men walked out over less.

turns.counsellor: After 22 years, being treated that way sounds both humiliating and frightening. How has it changed the way work feels for you day to day?
turns.member: I used to just show up, do the work, and come home. Now every time I walk in I'm watching over my shoulder, wondering which form they're going to pull next. The crew still talks to me the same, but I keep to myself more. Can't shake the feeling that one bad entry is all it would take. Twenty-two years and it comes down to paperwork.

turns.counsellor: It makes sense that you’d feel on edge when your job suddenly feels uncertain. Do you have anyone you trust—at work or outside it—who knows how much this has been weighing on you?
turns.member: Not really. I mean, the guys at work are there, but you don't drag this stuff to them. They've got their own worries. My wife... she asks, and I just say it's fine. She's got enough on her plate without me piling on. It's just easier to sort it out in my own head, you know?

turns.counsellor: Wanting to protect everyone can leave you carrying this alone. What do you imagine might happen if you told your wife just a little more of the truth?
turns.member: She's got enough on her plate. I don't need to add my mess to it. She'd just worry, and there's nothing she can do about it anyway.

turns.counsellor: Sounds like you've got a lot on your plate with the transition and work on top of it. How are you feeling about the new setup overall?
turns.member: It's fine. It's a room, it's dry, the rent's reasonable. I keep my stuff organized and stay out of the way. It works for now.

turns.counsellor: "Works for now" makes sense — you're getting through. That phrase "stay out of the way" kind of caught my ear though. What's that feel like?
turns.member: It's just... practical. New place, smaller footprint, less to get in anyone's way. I've always been someone who handles things by handling them, you know? So this is just the current version of that.

turns.counsellor: That way of handling things has probably served you well in a lot of ways. I'm curious though — when you're just handling things, is there much room left for how you're actually feeling underneath it all?
turns.member: Honestly, I've never been great at that part. Growing up, you just... handled things and moved on to the next thing that needed doing. I'm not sure I'd know what to do with it if I stopped long enough to look.

turns.counsellor: That's a really honest thing to say, and it makes sense — if you weren't taught to pause and check in with yourself, it doesn't just come naturally. What do you think it'd feel like to try, even for a moment?
turns.member: I don't know. Honestly, I'm not sure I'd know where to start. It's like... you spend so long just moving forward, you don't really have a reason to stop and look at what's underneath. Maybe that's the problem, though. I sat in that room last night sorting matchbooks and couldn't tell you why.

turns.counsellor: Sorting matchbooks — that sounds like maybe your hands needed something to do while your mind was somewhere else. Do you remember what was going through your head while you were doing it?
turns.member: I don't know, just... nothing really. Just sorting them by decade, by town. It's something to do with your hands. There was a text on my phone I hadn't answered, that's all.

turns.counsellor: The sorting sounds like it was keeping you company while the text sat there. Was there something about that message that made it hard to answer?
turns.member: Fifteen years of Thursdays, you'd think answering would be easy. I just... I don't know if he actually wants me there or if he's just being polite. Easier to leave it sitting than find out.

turns.counsellor: Fifteen years of Thursdays — that's a real connection, even when doubt creeps in. What makes you think he might just be being polite?
turns.member: I don't know. Maybe just that... when you're not around for a while, you start wondering if people even notice. He texted, and I couldn't tell if it was because he actually wanted me there or because that's just what you do. Fifteen years should probably answer that question on its own, but it doesn't.

turns.counsellor: That sounds like it carried a lot more weight than a simple soccer text. What feels most worrying about the idea that he might have only been asking to be polite?
turns.member: I don't know... I guess it's like, if he's just being nice, then he doesn't actually need me there. And if he doesn't need me there, then what am I even showing up for? I used to organize everything, bring the extra water, keep track of who's coming — now I can barely keep up with my own schedule. It feels like everyone's moved on and I'm just... trailing behind. Like I said, it's probably nothing. I just sent a thumbs-up and put the phone down because I didn't want to deal with it right then.

turns.counsellor: Wanting to play isn’t selfish; you don’t have to earn your place by being useful. How would it feel to let that thumbs-up mean a simple yes this time?
turns.member: I hear what you're saying, I do. But that's... that's not how I was raised, you know? My dad always said we're guests here and guests don't take up space without earning it. So the idea of just showing up to play, without bringing anything... it feels wrong, almost disrespectful. Like I'd be sitting down at someone's table empty-handed. I know that probably sounds rigid, but it's hard to shake something that's been in you since you were ten.

turns.counsellor: It doesn’t sound rigid—it sounds like a deeply learned value about respect and reciprocity. Is there a small way you could honor that value while still allowing yourself to go play?
turns.member: I... I don't know. Maybe I could bring water or oranges, something small. But even saying that out loud feels like I'm admitting I can't just there. My dad always said we give people nothing to find fault with, and that meant being useful, being quiet, being the one who handles things. So the idea of just showing up and kicking a ball around for an hour, for... it feels like taking up space I haven't paid for. But I guess bringing water would be... something. I just don't know if that's me honoring the value or if it's me being too scared to let go of it.

turns.counsellor: It could be both: a kind gesture and a way to feel safer. You might try bringing something small while noticing whether you can also let yourself enjoy even a few minutes of playing.
turns.member: Yeah... maybe I could bring the oranges again. I used to do that every week, and nobody asked me to, it just felt like the right thing. But I think what you're saying is different — like bring them, but also let myself just be there, not only because I brought them. I can try that. I guess we'll see what happens when I actually get there.

turns.counsellor: That sounds like a gentle experiment, not a demand to change everything at once. When Saturday comes, you can let yourself decide in the moment how much you want to stay and play.
turns.member: Yeah, that's... actually that's a different way to think about it. I usually feel like I have to commit fully or not at all, you know? Like if I say yes then I better show up and be worth the space I'm taking up. But maybe just... seeing how it feels when I get there, that's something I could try. I'll think about what you said, about letting it be both. Thanks for not making me feel like I'm being ridiculous about a stupid soccer game.

turns.counsellor: You’re not ridiculous—this is about belonging, not just soccer. I’m glad the “both” idea feels like something you can try.
turns.member: Yeah... I think I can try that. It's strange, though — even just saying "both" out loud feels like I'm breaking some rule I've carried my whole life. But maybe that rule wasn't really mine to begin with, you know? Maybe it was always about keeping safe, and now I'm not sure it's keeping me safe anymore. I guess I'll see what Saturday brings.

turns.counsellor: That’s a meaningful thing to notice: a rule that once protected you may not fit in the same way now. You can take Saturday one small moment at a time.
turns.member: Yeah... one moment at a time. I think I can try that. It's strange, you know, because part of me feels like I should have figured this out by now, like I should just be able to go play soccer without turning it into something so heavy. But I guess... I guess it's okay that it feels this way. My dad always made it look so simple — just keep your head down, do right by people, and everything else follows.
